My father hauled milk to the station the same as everybody up here did. There were nine families of us hauling to that station and we were in and out of each other's kitchens the whole year round and I could name you every one of them, but you don't want names, you want the trouble, they always want the trouble.
6	
7	The station stood at the very top of the Hollow where the road bends and then goes to nothing but the ridge. It was a low building, whitewashed, cold as a spring house inside even in August, and it smelled of milk and steam and hot iron, and you could hear the engine going before you came round the last turn. Ansel Keddie ran it. He went up there in ninety-five, the year before they opened it, to get it ready, and he tested that first summer too, and he was still there when I was a girl big enough to ride on the wagon with my father, so you can count that up and see how long a man can stand in one room.
8	
9	He kept a book. I want to say about that book because everybody knew about it, it wasn't any secret thing. It was ruled, and the ruling was his own, done with a straightedge, and every line in it was the same height as every other line, and his figures were like print. He wrote in it standing up at a slope desk by the window where the light came in. If a man came in and asked him what his milk had done, he did not have to hunt. He turned to the day and he read it off. He tested a thousand cans a week and never a blot in that book, and I heard my father say more than once that if the rest of the world kept its accounts the way Ansel Keddie kept his there would be no lawyers in Ashlin. Which was my father's way of talking. There are still lawyers in Ashlin.
10	
11	Now. Nineteen nineteen. That is the year everything went sour up here and I was seven years old and I remember it the way you remember a smell. A letter came from the Association, printed, over the manager's signature, and it said there was water in the cans coming down from Ostrey Hollow. That is what it said. Water in the cans. It went to nine families and my father was one of the nine and he read it at the table with his hat still on, which he never did, and my mother stood at the stove with her back to him and did not turn around the whole time he read it. He read it twice. Then he put it in the drawer of the desk in the front room and it was still in that drawer when he died and I believe my brother has it yet. Some of them kept theirs till they died. One woman I knew had hers pinned inside the lid of her trunk. You can tell people a thing like that is only business and they will still keep the paper forty years to prove what was said of them.
12

3	*Written out in numbered sections for the Association's own files, in the year after I laid down the minute book: from the minutes wherever the minutes will bear it, from my own recollection where they will not, and the two kept apart here as they ought to be kept.*
4	
5	**1. Of the organizing of the Association.** In 1889 the farmers of the Larrow Valley met at Larrow Green and organized themselves into the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association. Gideon Vose was elected the first president at that meeting and he held the office until 1911, which is twenty-two years, and no other man has held it so long. I did not see any of this. I was fourteen years old in 1889 and I came into the office as secretary in 1901, so for the first twelve years of the Association I am only a reader of its papers like anybody else, and a poorer reader than some, because the papers of exactly those years are the ones we have lost. The 1889–1892 minute book was lost when the office was moved in 1938. I say this here at the beginning because it governs everything I can and cannot write in the sections following.
6	
7	**2. Of the creamery at Larrow Green.** The main creamery was built at Larrow Green in 1891, on Larrow Creek, and it is the same building yet. Before it was built the members sold their milk where they could get a price for it and there was no common test and no common price, and every man's arithmetic was his own. The creamery ended that. Whatever is said of the Association afterward, it began as a plain remedy for a plain grievance, and I have never heard anybody in this valley say we should have been better without it.
8	
9	**3. Of the by-laws, and of Article VII.** Gideon Vose drafted the by-laws himself. He was not a lawyer and they read as a farmer wrote them, which is to their credit. The article that governs this history is the seventh, and because it is short and because it has been misquoted at me across this desk for forty years I set it down entire:
10	
11	> *Article VII. Every patron shall be paid for the milk he delivers according to the number of pounds of butter fat contained in it, ascertained by test, and not according to the weight of the milk; and the test of the station where he delivers shall govern.*
12	
13	Article VII was adopted at the annual meeting of 1892, the year after the creamery opened. What it did was this. Before it, a man was paid for what his cans weighed, and a hundred pounds of milk was a hundred pounds of milk whosever cow it came out of. After it, a man was paid for the fat that was found in his milk by a test made at the place where he delivered it, and the weight of his cans decided nothing by itself. The rule is a just rule and I have always said so: it pays a man for what he actually brings and not for the water that is naturally in it. But I would have the reader notice the last clause, which is the one nobody quotes. *The test of the station where he delivers shall govern.* Not the test of the creamery, not the average of the valley, not a test made over again anywhere else. The station's test, and no appeal from it. That clause is the hinge of the whole Ostrey Hollow business and it was written in 1892 by a man who died in 1917 and could not be asked about it afterward.
14	
15	**4. Of the officers in my time.** I was secretary from 1901 to 1940 and kept the minute book in my own hand throughout. Wilbur Teague came in as bookkeeper in 1905 and kept the ledgers. Hobart Sill was the buttermaker at Larrow Green and had the churn book and the cream receiving book. Selby Vose, son of the late president, was made manager in 1913 and served until 1938. ## Document Overview
Three retellings of a historical dispute (1889-1925) over milk testing practices in a rural valley, with traces extending to 1979. The conflict centered on Ansel Keddie, tester at Ostrey Hollow station, whose milk-test records showed consistently lower butterfat percentages than neighboring patrons' milk. The case resulted in an arbitration award with no admission of wrongdoing, a lasting family rift, and profound stigma affecting two people for decades.

## Cast of Characters and Relationships

**Ansel Keddie** (Tester, Ostrey Hollow station, 1896–1924)
- Ran the skimming station 7 miles up valley from Larrow Green
- Kept meticulous test books in his own hand, handwriting "like print," no blots across 29 seasons
- Married to Orra Keddie
- Denies taking cream: "I have never taken a pound of cream out of that station and there is not a man in this room who thinks I have when he is by himself" (March 1925 statement, revealing his awareness that people suspected him)
- Put out (fired) April 30, 1925, after arbitration award
- Died in the 1930s, still under stigma from the 1919 letter
- His question mark in the test book about the 1911 anomaly stood unanswered for 14 years

**Orra Keddie** (Ansel's wife)
- First cousin of old Mrs. Vose (wife of Association founder)
- Sister of Emmet Brant (largest milk patron, from Hessel Bottom)
- After 1919 letter, rift with her brother Emmet: "they did not speak. Not one word, not at the store, not at a funeral"
- Would walk to Larrow Green rather than pass her brother's lane
- Outlived Ansel and "had it the whole time" — the stigma — for years after his death
- The rift between Ansel and Emmet lasted "years and years" while they lived "within sight of each other's chimney smoke"
